cultivar: Plantation cultivars (Yabukita and related Japanese-origin varieties); some Hadong lots from native seedling bushes
processing: Leaf is shaded for a few weeks before harvest (less consistently than in Japan), steamed, dried without rolling into a flat tencha-style leaf, destemmed and stone-milled into a fine powder; cheaper culinary grades skip the shading.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) for the drinking grades; later picks go into culinary and latte powders.
appearance_dry: Fine, matte powder, bright to mid green in the drinking grades and a duller yellow-green in culinary ones.
appearance_liquor: Opaque bright green suspension with a fine foam when whisked.
appearance_wet: Not applicable: the powder is consumed whole; a well-whisked bowl shows no sediment until it settles.
taste_profile: Fresh and vegetal with a marine, spinach-like depth, a softer umami than Japanese koicha-grade matcha and a slightly firmer bitterness that lifts in a latte or with something sweet.

brewing.notes: Sift, then whisk with a bamboo whisk in a wide bowl until foamy. Korean tea ceremony tends to use a slightly thinner, cooler bowl than Japanese usucha; for lattes use 3 g and dissolve in a little hot water first.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring leaf, milled in small batches through the year and packed in tins or foil of 20–40 g, with a best-before date rather than a harvest grade. Powder fades faster than leaf: buy small tins, keep them sealed and cold, and finish a tin within a couple of months of opening.
description:
Malcha is Korea's powdered green tea, the same idea as Japanese matcha and spelt with the same characters. Powdered whisked tea was the court and temple tea of Goryeo Korea long before the modern Japanese style settled, then largely disappeared with the Joseon turn to leaf tea; what is sold today is a modern revival driven by the big Jeju and Boseong producers and by the café trade.

The process follows the Japanese model: shading the bushes before harvest to boost chlorophyll and amino acids, steaming, drying the leaf flat without rolling, and grinding it on stone mills. Shading varies by producer and is often said to be shorter and less rigorous than in Japan, so malcha can run a shade yellower and more vegetal than ceremonial Japanese matcha, and a lot of what is sold as malcha is unshaded culinary powder meant for lattes, ice cream and baking.

Whisked plain, a drinking-grade malcha is fresh, spinachy and marine with a gentle umami and a bitterness that is clean rather than harsh; it suits a thinner, cooler bowl than Japanese usucha and is lovely with Korean sweets. In a latte or over ice it holds its own against stronger flavours, which is where most of it ends up.

When buying, the grade words matter less than the colour and the price: a bright green, finely milled, pricier powder from a named Jeju or Boseong producer will be drinking quality; a dull yellow-green powder in a big bag is for cooking. Check the pack date, because powder oxidises quickly once opened.

If you want to see how Korea whisks tea, look for a darye (Korean tea ceremony) demonstration; the gestures are calmer and simpler than the Japanese ones, and the tea bowl is often a rough buncheong piece.
history:
Malcha is the Korean reading of 抹茶, the same word as Japanese matcha. Whisked powdered tea took shape in Song China and developed its shaded, bright green modern form in Japan; production has since spread to other countries, South Korea among them.

The specifically Korean record is thin for the modern product. What is clear is that demand is recent and strong: in 2025 Korean food companies and cafés rushed out matcha-flavoured products. The word on a pack does not guarantee shading or stone milling, and much powder sold this way is meant for lattes and baking.
